The video explains how AI GPUs like Nvidia's H100 and AMD's B100 depend on a long, fragile global supply chain, from ultra‑pure raw materials to a handful of advanced chip foundries and specialized tool makers.

Key stages in the AI chip chain
Demand for AI data centers has caused Nvidia and AMD revenues to surge, making reliable access to GPUs a strategic bottleneck for cloud providers and AI labs.

The chain is broken into three main steps: raw materials (especially high‑purity quartz for silicon wafers plus metals like copper, aluminum, and tin), chip design by fabless and integrated device manufacturers, and manufacturing in a few leading foundries.

Raw materials and concentration
AI chips start from silicon derived from very high‑purity quartz (HPQ), much of which currently comes from a single major source in Spruce Pine, North Carolina, creating a potential choke point if supply is disrupted.

China is trying to reduce dependence on U.S. HPQ by developing its own deposits and broader materials supply, but still relies heavily on imports for the highest grades.

Design, IP, and geopolitics
Companies like Nvidia, AMD, Apple, Amazon, Google, and Microsoft are fabless: they design complex GPUs and accelerators with tens to hundreds of billions of transistors but outsource manufacturing, while Samsung and Intel both design and fabricate chips.

Critical design IP and tools come from firms such as ARM, Synopsys, and Cadence, which complicates China's push for semiconductor independence, especially under strict U.S. export controls affecting Huawei, SMIC, and other Chinese players.

Foundries and bottlenecks
Only a few companies (TSMC in Taiwan, Samsung in South Korea, SMIC in China, and Intel in the U.S.) can manufacture cutting‑edge chips at 3–5 nm and below, with processes involving steps like photolithography, etching, and packaging.

The tightest bottleneck is extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography, where a single company, ASML in the Netherlands, provides the multi‑hundred‑million‑dollar scanners required, making access to ASML tools and advanced foundry capacity a key axis of U.S.–China tech competition.

"The Philippines should not reject a potentially transformative technology-industrial opportunity simply because it is difficult. It should negotiate the conditions that make the investment beneficial, sustainable, and fair."
And there is an important distinction between taking the opportunity and blindly accepting every condition.
What would give us reasonable assurance?
There should be at least six guarantees:
Water security — industrial water requirements must not undermine farmers or communities. New water infrastructure should have clearly allocated sources and priority protections for essential domestic and agricultural needs.
Reliable and affordable energy — the project should not simply consume existing electricity and make power more expensive for everyone else. Generation and transmission capacity should expand alongside industrial demand.
Farmers must be participants, not casualties — affected farmers should receive fair compensation, relocation or livelihood programs where applicable, and opportunities to participate in the new economy through training, employment, supply chains, or other arrangements.
Environmental safeguards must be enforceable — not merely promises in an investment presentation. Water use, wastewater, land conversion, emissions, waste disposal and ecological impacts need measurable standards and independent monitoring.
The government must control its financial exposure — a $70-billion potential ecosystem should not become a situation where taxpayers bear most of the infrastructure cost while private investors capture most of the benefits. The financing and risk-sharing arrangements need transparency.
Technology and human-capital development must be part of the deal — Filipinos should not merely provide land, utilities and labor while the high-value intellectual property, engineering and research remain elsewhere. Universities, technical schools, R&D, semiconductor engineering, AI, electronics and advanced manufacturing should be deliberately integrated into the ecosystem.
The most important point
Your argument becomes much stronger if you change the question from:
"Should we accept Pax Silica or protect our farmers?"
"Can we design Pax Silica so that farmers, workers, investors, communities and the next generation of Filipinos all participate in the benefits?"
That is the balance of sustainable progress you are describing.
There will inevitably be disruption. Some land may have competing uses. Infrastructure will cost money. Water and electricity will have opportunity costs. Some communities may have to adjust. Some promised jobs may take years to materialize.
So nobody should promise farmers:
"Don't worry. Everything will be fine."
A responsible government should instead say:
"We recognize what you could lose, we will measure those risks, and we will put legally enforceable protections in place before development proceeds."
At the same time, it would also be reasonable to tell Filipino parents:
"We cannot protect today's economic structure forever if doing so prevents our children from entering tomorrow's industries."
That is the difficult balance.
And there is one more safeguard I would add
Do not judge Pax Silica solely by the initial $70 billion figure.
The critical question is whether the first investment creates an ecosystem that subsequently attracts semiconductor companies, advanced manufacturers, AI companies, electronics firms, research institutions, engineering centers and other suppliers.
If it does, the economic multiplier over 20–30 years could be substantially more important than the initial investment.
But that outcome should be treated as a potential, not a guarantee.
So I would phrase your conclusion this way:
The Philippines should neither blindly accept nor reflexively reject Pax Silica. It should negotiate from the position that this may be a once-in-a-generation opportunity, while demanding enforceable safeguards for water, energy, farmers, communities, the environment, public finances and Filipino participation.
The objective should not be simply to attract $70 billion. The objective should be to use the investment as a foundation for a Philippine technology-industrial ecosystem that can still be creating opportunities for Filipino children 20 or 30 years from now.
That is what sustainable progress means: protecting what we have today while building what the next generation will need tomorrow..

Pax Silica: The Philippines Must Debate the Future Based on Facts, Not Fear
Throughout Philippine history, there have been many instances when our country hesitated to embrace emerging industries and transformative technologies, only to realize years later that our neighbors had already built the expertise, industries, and wealth that we were still debating. We cannot afford to repeat that mistake.
The world is changing at a pace unprecedented in modern history. Artificial intelligence, robotics, semiconductor manufacturing, advanced computing, automation, and quantum technologies are no longer futuristic concepts. They are today's strategic industries, driving economic growth, national competitiveness, military capability, healthcare innovation, scientific research, and the digital transformation of governments and businesses around the world.
Whether we like it or not, these industries will define the global economy for the next fifty years.
The real question is not whether the Philippines should participate.
The real question is whether we intend to become active participants in this technological revolution or remain consumers of technologies developed by other nations.
The Debate Has Become Too Political
Unfortunately, much of the public discussion surrounding Pax Silica has become dominated by politics, speculation, and emotional rhetoric rather than objective analysis.
Some commentators have raised environmental concerns, while others immediately portray the project as either a miracle investment or a national threat. Both extremes oversimplify a highly complex undertaking.
Environmental protection is a legitimate concern. Every major industrial project should undergo rigorous environmental review, scientific impact assessments, transparent regulation, and continuous monitoring. The proper response to environmental risks is not to dismiss them, but neither is it to assume that such risks cannot be managed. Modern engineering exists precisely to reduce, monitor, and mitigate environmental impacts through design, technology, regulation, and responsible operations.
What is largely missing from public discussion is the engineering perspective.
Too few commentators explain how AI infrastructure operates, what semiconductor manufacturing actually requires, how data centers consume and recycle energy, what supply chains are needed, how advanced manufacturing ecosystems are developed, or what technical skills Filipino engineers must acquire to participate competitively.
Instead of educating the public, many discussions are reduced to political narratives, ideological arguments, or speculative conclusions unsupported by engineering or industrial analysis.
The Questions Journalists Should Be Asking
Rather than inviting commentators to speculate, journalists should be asking questions that help the public understand the realities of building an advanced technology industry.
For example:
Can the Philippines provide reliable and affordable electricity required for AI infrastructure and semiconductor manufacturing?
Will renewable energy, nuclear power, or conventional power generation be sufficient to sustain future demand?
What water management technologies will be implemented to minimize environmental impact?
Can local industries supply construction materials, precision components, electronic parts, logistics, and maintenance services?
Do Philippine universities currently produce enough engineers, computer scientists, data specialists, material scientists, and technicians to meet future demand?
What additional educational reforms are needed to prepare students for these industries?
What incentives will encourage multinational companies to establish research and development facilities rather than limiting operations to assembly or data hosting?
How will intellectual property created through research collaborations benefit Filipino institutions and companies?
These are the conversations that help a nation prepare for the future.
The Most Valuable Investment Is Knowledge
Perhaps the most overlooked aspect of Pax Silica is not the buildings, equipment, or financial investment.
It is knowledge transfer.
History demonstrates that industrialization is fundamentally a process of acquiring knowledge.
When foreign companies establish sophisticated operations, local engineers, technicians, scientists, managers, suppliers, and universities gain opportunities to learn technologies that would otherwise take decades to develop independently.
If structured properly, projects such as Pax Silica could provide:
Hands-on experience for Filipino engineers, software developers, scientists, and technicians.
Research collaboration between Philippine universities and internationally recognized technology companies.
Training in artificial intelligence, robotics, semiconductor fabrication, automation, cybersecurity, cloud computing, and advanced manufacturing.
Development of local engineering firms, technology startups, and component suppliers.
Creation of high-value jobs capable of reducing the continuing migration of Filipino professionals overseas.
Opportunities for Filipino researchers to participate in international innovation networks instead of remaining primarily consumers of foreign technologies.
Knowledge compounds over time.
A generation of well-trained engineers eventually becomes innovators, entrepreneurs, educators, researchers, and industry leaders capable of creating entirely new industries.
Every Industrial Nation Followed a Similar Path
No country became an industrial power by waiting until it possessed all the necessary expertise.
Japan imported Western technology during the Meiji Restoration.
South Korea attracted foreign investment while aggressively educating its engineers.
Taiwan developed its semiconductor industry through partnerships between government, universities, and international firms.
Singapore invested heavily in education, infrastructure, and research before becoming a global technology hub.
China initially welcomed foreign manufacturers, learned from international partnerships, and steadily developed domestic technological capabilities.
None of these countries relied solely on imported technology forever.
They transformed technology transfer into domestic innovation.
That transformation required long-term planning, disciplined investment in education, and an unwavering commitment to developing their own human capital.
What Success Should Actually Look Like
The success of Pax Silica should not be measured simply by the amount of foreign investment announced or the number of buildings constructed.
its true success should be measured by outcomes such as:
Filipino engineers designing world-class technologies.
Philippine universities conducting internationally respected AI and semiconductor research.
Local companies joining global technology supply chains.
Filipino-owned technology firms exporting products and services worldwide.
Growth in patents, scientific publications, and locally developed intellectual property.
A significant reduction in the migration of highly skilled Filipino professionals seeking opportunities abroad.
These are indicators of genuine industrial development.
A Decision That Will Shape Generations
Every generation encounters opportunities that determine its economic future.
Previous generations debated electronics manufacturing, automotive production, aerospace development, and large-scale semiconductor expansion while neighboring countries moved decisively and built globally competitive industries.
The Philippines should study those experiences—not to assign blame, but to avoid repeating the same pattern.
Supporting innovation does not require abandoning environmental responsibility, national security, or public accountability.
Likewise, exercising caution should not become an excuse for rejecting opportunities before they have been thoroughly evaluated.
The objective should be neither blind optimism nor automatic opposition.
It should be informed judgment based on engineering, economics, education, science, and the long-term national interest.
If Pax Silica ultimately delivers meaningful technology transfer, advanced engineering education, research collaboration, industrial capability, and a competitive technology ecosystem, it could become one of the most consequential investments in Philippine history.
If it fails to achieve those objectives, the Philippines risks remaining primarily a host for foreign infrastructure rather than becoming a nation that designs, invents, manufactures, and exports technologies of its own.
The decision before us is therefore much larger than a single investment project.
It is a decision about what kind of nation we want to become.
Will we continue importing the technologies of the future, or will we begin developing the engineers, scientists, researchers, entrepreneurs, and industries capable of creating them?
That is the debate the Filipino people deserve.

While dominant architectures like superconducting systems require extreme cooling colder than deep space (~15 millikelvin), several alternative quantum technologies operate natively at room temperature.

Room-Temperature Quantum Systems

Photonic Quantum Computers: These systems use photons (light particles) as qubits. Companies like Xanadu and QuiX Quantum build universal optical quantum computers that fit into standard, uncooled data center racks. Note that while the processor itself runs at room temperature, some photonic setups still use minor cooling for high-performance light detectors.

Neutral Atom Systems: This architecture uses lasers (optical tweezers) to trap individual atoms in place. Companies like PASQAL have built 100+ qubit systems that operate entirely on laboratory tables without billion-dollar refrigeration setups. 

Trapped Ion Systems: Providers like IonQ use a technique called Doppler cooling—where targeted lasers slow down atoms to lower their temperature directly, eliminating the need for bulky, external cryogenic containment.

We see planets by the billions.
We see chemistry everywhere.

Not one.
Not a whisper.

This silence is not an accident.
It is a consequence of the universe's own evolutionary machinery.

Life began on Earth almost as soon as the planet cooled. The moment water pooled, chemistry ignited. Microbial life appeared so quickly that it seems less like a miracle and more like a reflex — something the universe does automatically when given the right ingredients.

If the cosmos is a garden, then microbial life is its moss.
It grows everywhere.

But moss does not write symphonies.
Moss does not build telescopes.
Moss does not wonder why it exists.

For that, something far stranger is required.

The Second Truth: Intelligence Is Not the Goal of Evolution
For 165 million years, dinosaurs ruled Earth. They were magnificent, diverse, adaptive, and utterly dominant. They filled every niche, from ocean to sky. They survived climate swings, volcanic winters, and shifting continents.

And in all that time — nearly two hundred million years — not one of them invented a symbol.
Not one carved a tool.
Not one wrote a word.

Evolution does not reward thought.
It rewards survival.

And survival, in a stable ecosystem, belongs to armor, claws, speed, venom, and specialization. Nature converges again and again on the same forms — crabs, shells, teeth, talons — because these are the shapes that win the game.

A brain is expensive.
A brain is slow.
A brain is fragile.
A brain is a liability in a world of predators.

The universe is not a cradle for minds.
It is an endless, thriving aquarium of armored creatures locked in a perpetual arms race.

The Third Truth: Minds Require Catastrophe
If intelligence is to emerge, the arms race must be broken.

On Earth, it took a cosmic bullet — a rock six miles wide — to shatter the dinosaur empire. The impact did not sterilize the planet, but it did something just as important:

It killed the giants.

It killed the armored titans who had dominated the world for millions of years.
It cleared the stage.

And in the ashes, the meek survived — small, warm-blooded, flexible creatures who could eat anything, hide anywhere, and adapt to everything.

Only when the world was emptied of claws did the brain become a viable strategy.

Intelligence was not the next step.
It was the last resort.

The Fourth Truth: There Are Different Ways to Make a Mind
Across the universe, there are only two escape hatches from the endless cycle of armor and claws:

1. The Reset Path — The Meek Inherit the Earth
A planet must experience a perfectly tuned catastrophe:

Big enough to kill the apex predators

Small enough to spare the undergrowth

Timed precisely after complex life evolves

Followed by a long period of stability

This is the path Earth took.

2. The Fluke Path — The Stoned Dinosaur
If no catastrophe occurs, the only remaining route is a biochemical miracle:

A symbiotic fungus

A parasitic neural mutation

A runaway social arms race

A dietary shift that rewires cognition

This path is so rare it borders on myth.

And yet, mathematically, it must exist — because the universe is vast, and life is creative.

But both paths are so improbable that when we fold them into the physics of planet formation, the odds collapse to a single number:

One mind per ten million galaxies.

The Fifth Truth: Time Is the Final Knife
Even if a galaxy produces one civilization in its entire 10‑billion‑year lifespan, that civilization only shines for a moment — a flicker in cosmic time.

If a technological species lasts 100 million years, it occupies just 1% of its galaxy's history.

That means:

99% of galaxies that ever birthed a mind are silent right now.

To find another consciousness alive at the same moment as us, we must search not one galaxy, not a hundred, but millions.

When we map this onto the actual density of galaxies in our region of the universe, the answer is staggering:

Our nearest active neighbor is likely 2.5 billion light-years away.

Far beyond our supercluster.
Far beyond any hope of communication.
Far beyond the reach of our entire species.

We are alone in every direction the eye can see.

The Final Truth: Consciousness Is the Universe Waking Up
If the math is right — and every line of evidence suggests it is — then the human mind is not a trivial accident.

It is the rarest structure, the single most plex expression in nature of the distillation of that 13.8-billion-year-old quark and gluon soup the universe has ever produced that we know of.

A brain is not just a biological organ.
It is the cosmos folding itself into awareness.
It is the universe looking back at itself through your eyes.

And because minds are so rare, compassion is not optional.
It is the only rational response.

When something is unique, you protect it.
When something is irreplaceable, you cherish it.
When something is fragile, you guard it fiercely.

Human consciousness is a flame in a desert of darkness.
If we let it go out, the universe loses its ability to understand itself for billions of light-years.

We are the eyes of the cosmos.
We are the only voice for unimaginable distances.
We are the custodians of the rarest treasure in existence.

And we must keep the flame alive with love.

Apple faced a similar wave of problems when they tried to set up American manufacturing for MacBook Air laptops. For instance, they couldn't get the high-precision screws needed for the cases. The only manufacturer capable of producing them at volume was using 70-year-old machines that lacked the tight tolerances and couldn't handle the bends at the required size. Apple ended up flying in cargo jets full of just those screws for the production line. They also struggled to find enough production engineers in the entire United States, managing to hire only three, none of whom had the necessary high-precision manufacturing experience, and they could only cover half the shifts. In China, if there's a production issue, you can call the nearby dorms and have 20 production engineers on the line in 20 minutes. This video, featuring Chris Miller, author of Chip War, explores the extreme complexity and critical importance of the semiconductor industry in modern technology. Here is a summary of the key takeaways:

1. The Complexity of Chip Manufacturing:
•	Semiconductors are harder to make than nuclear weapons: While nuclear technology has stagnated since the 1960s, chip technology has advanced at an unprecedented rate, making them both tiny and inexpensive (0:00-0:36).
•	Atomic Precision: Manufacturing involves carving billions of microscopic transistors onto silicon wafers. This requires absolute purity in materials and state-of-the-art lithography tools (2:02-3:03, 14:24-15:21).
•	Specialized Supply Chains: No single company can produce an advanced chip alone. It requires a global network of specialized partners for materials, software, and highly complex equipment (6:45-7:20).

2. The Economics of Scale and Moore's Law:
•	Moore's Law: Though not a physical law, it is an economic driver predicting that transistor density—and thus computing power—doubles roughly every two years. This has enabled the ubiquity of computing in everything from smartphones to appliances (8:37-9:43, 11:02-11:40).
•	Barriers to Entry: A single cutting-edge chip facility can cost $20 billion. Consequently, the industry has consolidated, with only a few companies worldwide capable of competing at the highest level (5:54-6:15, 15:33-16:05).
•	TSMC's Dominance: The Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) manufactures approximately 90% of the world's most advanced processor chips because their massive scale and data-driven learning allow them to be both cheaper and more advanced than competitors (5:30-5:49, 16:06-16:26).

3. Future Outlook:
•	As shrinking transistors in 2D becomes harder, the industry is shifting toward 3D stacking of transistors to continue increasing computing power (13:46-14:19).
•	Despite some debates about the slowing of Moore's Law, specialized chips for AI are currently maintaining that historic pace of innovation (12:24-12:46).

If we look only at the workers who could potentially be displaced by AI, we see the problem—but not the larger economic transition taking place.
The Philippines cannot assume that the BPO model of the past will remain unchanged indefinitely. The real question is not simply how many BPO jobs might be affected, but what kinds of jobs will replace them and whether Filipinos are prepared to move into those jobs.
This is where Pax Silica deserves to be considered as part of a much larger development strategy.
Pax Silica is being presented not simply as another industrial park, but as an advanced manufacturing and logistics ecosystem connected to the global AI and technology value chain. The Philippine government has described the proposed hub in precisely those terms, including advanced manufacturing, logistics and quality employment.
Therefore, saying:
"What about the 6,000 farmers?"or
"What about BPO workers who may be displaced?"are legitimate questions—but they are only the beginning of the analysis.
The answer should not be to disregard the 6,000 farmers or BPO workers. They deserve protection, compensation, retraining and a realistic pathway into the emerging economy.But protecting today's jobs cannot mean refusing to prepare for tomorrow's economy.Development policy has to look at both sides of the transition: who may lose opportunities today, and what opportunities we can create for them and their children tomorrow. Targets include monazite and xenotime, which are important sources of rare earth elements, alongside rutile and zircon. Fieldwork reportedly found strongly monazite-enriched alluvial material. 
✅* Mugheb watershed: A 2026 peer-reviewed study found total rare-earth concentrations of roughly 215–458 mg/kg in alluvial sediments, with notable La, Ce, Pr, Nd, Gd and Sm. The researchers describe the sediments as a potentially promising unconventional REE resource, but emphasize that further assessment is needed before economic viability can be established. 
✅* Ediki River, Douala Basin: Another 2026 study identified 127–310 mg/kg total REEs in black shale, again predominantly light rare earths. The authors characterize this as a potential unconventional resource requiring further exploration.
✅ Crude oil (petroleum): A long-established producing resource; Cameroon has exported oil since 1977. 
✅Natural gas:Cameroon has substantial identified natural-gas resources and an established gas/LNG industry. 
✅Iron ore: Large deposits have been identified, including Mbalam and deposits around Kribi. Cameroon began commissioning major iron-ore projects in 2025. 
✅Bauxite: Cameroon has major bauxite deposits, particularly around Minim-Martap and Ngaoundal. The Minim-Martap project entered the country's producing-mining sector in 2025. 
✅Gold: Gold is currently produced, particularly through artisanal and small-scale mining. USGS recorded about 855 kg of contained gold production in 2024. 
✅Diamonds: Cameroon has documented diamond deposits and ongoing artisanal/small-scale diamond production. 
✅Cobalt: Significant cobalt deposits are documented, especially around Lomié/Nkamouna in eastern Cameroon. 
✅Nickel: Nickel occurs alongside cobalt and manganese in the Lomié area. 
✅Manganese: Documented deposits, including in association with the Lomié-Nkamouna mineral project. 
✅Rutile / ilmenite: Titanium-bearing mineral deposits have been identified, including the Akonolinga rutile deposit. 
✅Limestone: Significant limestone resources are used for cement and other construction applications. 
✅Marble: Marble deposits, including around Bidzar, are documented; an industrial marble project entered production in 2025.

The race for semiconductor supremacy has become one of the most critical global competitions, as semiconductors are the backbone of modern technology, powering everything from smartphones and computers to advanced military systems and renewable energy infrastructure. The COVID-19 pandemic exposed the vulnerabilities in the global semiconductor supply chain, underscoring their importance in national security and economic stability. As a result, countries around the world, including the US, China, and members of the European Union, are prioritizing investments in semiconductor manufacturing and research to reduce dependence on foreign suppliers and bolster their technological sovereignty.

Semiconductors are integral to the development of next-generation technologies, including artificial intelligence, quantum computing, and autonomous vehicles, all of which will shape the future of global economies and geopolitics. In the race for dominance, countries are investing heavily in both increasing production capacity and advancing the technology itself, such as through the development of smaller, more efficient chips that can handle more complex computations with greater energy efficiency.

The competition is also driven by the geopolitical tensions surrounding supply chains and technology leadership. For instance, the US has implemented policies like the CHIPS Act, which incentivize domestic semiconductor production and research, aiming to reduce reliance on Asian manufacturers. Similarly, China has made significant strides in its semiconductor capabilities, although it still faces challenges in key areas such as advanced chip manufacturing.

The semiconductor race is not only about economic growth but also about national security. As chips are used in a wide array of military technologies, controlling semiconductor production is seen as a way to safeguard against cyber threats and other strategic vulnerabilities. 

However, this race also raises important questions about global trade, environmental impact, and the ethical considerations of monopolistic practices in the tech industry. The concentration of semiconductor production in a few countries or companies could lead to imbalances, with potential consequences for smaller economies and consumers.

In conclusion, the semiconductor race is not just a technological competition but also a strategic, economic, and geopolitical contest. The outcome will determine the direction of technological development, the balance of global power, and the ability of nations to innovate and protect their interests in an increasingly digital world. For the future, investment in research, diversification of supply chains, and international cooperation will be key to ensuring that the benefits of semiconductor innovation are shared equitably and sustainably.

I have long regarded you as a respected economist whose work on public finance, governance, environmental policy, and accountability has contributed significantly to Philippine public discourse. Your perspective on environmental stewardship is important and deserves serious consideration.

However, Pax Silica presents issues that extend well beyond economics and environmental policy alone.

During my professional career, I served as Chief Accountant for one of the major suppliers of electronic components serving companies in Silicon Valley. Although I was not an engineer, my work gave me a unique opportunity to observe how advanced manufacturing, semiconductor production, engineering, finance, logistics, supply-chain management, and technological innovation operate as an integrated ecosystem. After retirement, I have continued to learn from my daughter and son-in-law, both of whom work in Silicon Valley's technology sector and have shared with me their experiences about the industry's working environment, technological culture, and continuous innovation.

Because of that exposure, I believe Pax Silica raises questions that require a broader and more interdisciplinary discussion than we have seen so far.

The project involves semiconductor manufacturing, artificial intelligence infrastructure, data centers, industrial engineering, power systems, water resource management, advanced computing, cybersecurity, logistics, workforce development, and long-term industrial planning. No single discipline can adequately evaluate all of these dimensions.

For that reason, I believe the public discussion would benefit from hearing not only economists and environmental advocates, but also semiconductor engineers, computer scientists, AI researchers, electrical engineers, environmental engineers, industrial planners, energy specialists, data-center architects, supply-chain executives, and professionals who have firsthand experience working in technology ecosystems such as Silicon Valley, Taiwan, South Korea, Japan, Singapore, and other advanced industrial economies.

As an economist, you understand the importance of gathering evidence before reaching conclusions.

Perhaps journalists should also investigate another side of the story by interviewing Filipino computer scientists, semiconductor engineers, AI specialists, and other professionals currently working in these global technology centers.

They could ask practical questions such as:

What skills are most in demand in today's AI and semiconductor industries?
How do universities prepare graduates for these careers?
What is the working environment inside leading technology companies?
What opportunities exist for research, innovation, and professional growth?
What salary ranges can young engineers reasonably expect as their careers progress?
What standard of living do these careers provide—not to sensationalize income, but to understand the economic value of highly skilled technical professions?
Most importantly, what knowledge and experience could be transferred to the Philippines if projects like Pax Silica are designed with education and technology transfer as central objectives?

These questions are not about glorifying Silicon Valley or comparing lifestyles, but I can say, Computer Science Engineers are compensated not a mechanic but   Engineers. 

They are about understanding what has enabled advanced technology economies to produce generations of world-class engineers, innovators, entrepreneurs, and scientists.

If the Philippines can create opportunities for its own young engineers to acquire comparable knowledge, experience, and technical expertise without having to leave their families or seek employment abroad, that alone would represent a significant national achievement.

The greatest long-term value of Pax Silica may not be measured by the billions of pesos invested or the number of buildings constructed.

It may ultimately be measured by the generation of Filipino engineers, scientists, researchers, and entrepreneurs who gain the knowledge, confidence, and opportunity to build the next generation of Philippine technology. The Cult of Certainty: How Scientism Mistakes Symbols for Reality

Abstract

This essay dismantles the illusion of scientific and mathematical authority over reality. It argues that physics, mathematics, and cosmology have become modern priesthoods—fluent in symbols, blind to their own assumptions, and convinced that their linguistic constructions constitute the world itself. Beneath their precision lies an unacknowledged act of faith: the belief that their frameworks, born of human limitation, can speak for the infinite complexity of Nature.

1. Introduction: The Rise of a New Dogma

Where religion once claimed the cosmos, scientism now reigns. Its prophets wear lab coats instead of robes, its scriptures are peer-reviewed, and its miracles are equations. It promises salvation through measurement, yet forgets that every instrument was built by fallible hands, every metric chosen by fallible minds.

Science is not the problem; its humility is. Scientism—the conviction that empirical method alone exhausts reality—is philosophy dressed in the armor of precision, mistaking its own reflection for the world.

2. The Frame That Sees Only Itself

Every experiment begins with a premise: what to measure, how to measure, what counts as real. Instruments do not reveal Nature; they negotiate with it, returning answers framed by the questions we taught them to ask.

To believe otherwise is to mistake a telescope for the stars. The data that scientists prize as "objective" already arrive pre-filtered through design, expectation, and interpretation. What emerges as "fact" is not a message from Nature but a conversation among humans—mediated by language, technology, and theory.

Scientism hides this circularity behind jargon and precision. Its practitioners forget that a system cannot justify its own axioms; the framework that defines observation cannot step outside itself to claim omniscience.

3. Mathematics: The Most Beautiful Pretend Game Ever Played

Mathematics is sublime—but it is also make-believe. Its truths are conditional: if these axioms, then those conclusions. When physicists write the cosmos in equations, they are translating mystery into grammar. The translation is elegant, but it is not the thing itself.

To claim that "the universe is mathematical" is to commit linguistic idolatry. Numbers describe patterns; they do not explain being. The formula E=mc² predicts the behavior of matter and energy—it does not tell us what matter or energy are. The certainty of mathematics is the certainty of definition, not of reality.

Einstein himself warned against this confusion: the moment mathematics becomes certain, it ceases to refer to the world. The moment it refers to the world, it ceases to be certain.

4. The Mirage of Empirical Authority

Modern physics and cosmology are cathedrals built on inference. Dark matter, dark energy, singularities, strings—none of these have been seen. They are invoked to preserve the internal coherence of equations that cannot account for observed phenomena. These invisible entities are not discoveries but placeholders for ignorance, named and worshipped as though naming made them real.

The irony is exquisite: in fleeing metaphysics, science reinvented it. It simply changed the vocabulary. Where theologians spoke of the divine, cosmologists now speak of the singularity; both point to something unobservable that explains everything else.

5. Consciousness: The One Fact That Cannot Be Denied

All observation presupposes an observer. Before there is data, there is awareness. Before there is theory, there is experience. To reduce consciousness to neural noise or quantum computation is to saw off the branch upon which knowledge sits.

Science studies phenomena within consciousness while pretending to stand outside it. But consciousness is the condition of the entire enterprise—the light by which all "facts" are seen. Without it, there is no experiment, no equation, no universe as such.

Thus, consciousness is not an afterthought of matter but its precondition. Every attempt to explain awareness as an emergent property of blind particles is a failure to recognize that "blind particles" are themselves ideas appearing in awareness.

6. The Human Element: Experts, Priests, and Pretenders

The "expert" class often claims to speak for reality itself, as though a PhD confers divine insight. Yet their authority rests on consensus, not revelation. Peer review replaces peer thinking; specialization rewards obedience over insight.

Academia has become a hierarchy of sanctioned ignorance—brilliant minds confined to narrow tunnels, mistaking the light at the end for the sun. Their jargon is a fortress built to defend not truth but prestige. To question them is to be labeled "unscientific," a modern form of heresy.

But no title or theorem exempts a human from the same fleshly frailty that binds us all. Every calculation, every cosmological model, is written by a primate briefly conscious on a tiny planet, staring into an abyss and mistaking its own reflection for the infinite.

7. Conclusion: The Return to Wonder

Science is a method. Reality is an experience. To confuse the two is to turn curiosity into creed. The universe does not speak in equations; it speaks in being.

The humility proper to inquiry is not the arrogance of certainty but the recognition that the map will never become the territory. Our instruments may refine the contours of what is measurable, but the immeasurable remains—the mystery that births both observer and observation.

*No one disputes the practical applications of science, utility is not contested. The task is not to abolish science, but to restore perspective: to remember that the finger pointing to the moon is not the moon, and that the most perfect formula will always fall short of describing the fact that anything exists at all.*

Reality cannot be owned by a discipline, only encountered by a consciousness.

Why It Is Impossible to Produce Indisputable Evidence That Nature Is Not Infinite

1. You cannot prove non-existence beyond observational horizons.

Physics is bounded by observational limits:

Cosmic horizon

Particle horizon

Measurement precision

Quantum decoherence boundaries

Anything outside these horizons is not empirically accessible even in theory.

Thus, any claim of a "finite Nature" requires absolute knowledge of what lies beyond all possible observation — which is impossible.

You cannot prove a boundary you cannot detect.

Win Gatchalian. In any case, it is imperative that the Senate Committee on Environment pursue further investigations on exactly what types of mineral processing companies are on the discussion table as part of the Philippine's Pax Silica contribution. There is a very wide gap between the mineral ores that are currently being pulled out of the Philippine ground and the input to the semiconductor fabrication facilities that the Clark hub is proposing to capture. Unfortunately, this very wide gap can only be filled with the current smelting technologies that leave behind very serious environmental consequences (land, water and air pollution). The Phil government must proactively create a firm and comprehensive requirement to address these serious environmental concerns during negotiations with prospective investor companies who will build and operate the mineral processing plants. During the press conference, representatives of the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) explained the vision behind the project. BCDA is a government-owned corporation established under Republic Act No. 7227 on March 13, 1992, with the mandate of transforming former military bases into centers of economic growth and investment.

The Philippines has never lacked intelligent people. However, much of the public discussion has understandably focused on the possible risks and environmental implications of the project. Those concerns deserve careful consideration, but they should be complemented by an equally thorough examination of the potential economic, technological, educational, and industrial benefits that projects like Pax Silica could bring to the country.

What the Philippines needs is a broader and more substantive discussion—one that draws upon the knowledge and experience of individuals who have actually built, operated, managed, and worked within world-class technology ecosystems.

Their insights are valuable because they understand not only the technical aspects of semiconductor manufacturing, artificial intelligence, advanced electronics, research and development, and innovation, but also the institutional, financial, educational, and industrial foundations required to make such ecosystems successful.

Constructive criticism is essential for any major national initiative. However, criticism is most valuable when it is informed by practical experience and a clear understanding of how globally competitive technology hubs are built, operated, and sustained.

If Pax Silica moves forward, it should not be viewed merely as another investment project. It should become a long-term national strategy for developing Filipino engineers, scientists, researchers, innovators, entrepreneurs, and globally competitive technology industries. Its success should ultimately be measured not only by the investments it attracts, but by the knowledge it creates, the industries it builds, the high-value jobs it generates, and the opportunities it provides for future generations of Filipinos.

That is the broader conversation the country should be having—not simply whether the project should proceed, but how it can be implemented successfully so that it becomes a transformative milestone in the Philippines' industrial and technological development.

Perhaps you could also examine another side of the story.

The public discussion would benefit greatly from interviews with Filipino computer scientists, semiconductor engineers, AI specialists, data center architects, electrical engineers, industrial planners, and other professionals currently working in some of the world's leading technology ecosystems, including Silicon Valley, Taiwan, South Korea, Japan, and Singapore.

These professionals possess firsthand knowledge of how advanced technology industries actually operate. Their experience could help Filipinos better understand the engineering, industrial, educational, and economic realities behind projects such as Pax Silica.

Rather than spending valuable intellectual energy debating political positions or focusing primarily on what might go wrong, why not broaden the conversation by asking what must be done for the Philippines to succeed?

For example:

What technical skills will be most critical in the AI and semiconductor industries over the next twenty years?
What kind of engineering and scientific talent will the Philippines need?
How can Philippine universities better prepare students for these careers?
What forms of technology transfer should the government negotiate with global partners?
How can Filipino companies become part of the global semiconductor and AI supply chains?
What environmental safeguards have proven effective in countries with mature technology industries?
How can the Philippines ensure that projects like Pax Silica produce innovators, researchers, and technology entrepreneurs—not merely a workforce engaged in routine manufacturing?

These are the questions that can elevate the national conversation.

A project of this scale deserves to be evaluated through the lenses of engineering, economics, environmental science, industrial policy, education, and long-term national strategy—not solely through politics or speculation.

I would also respectfully recommend a different approach to communicating the project to the public.

Rather than relying primarily on PowerPoint presentations, consider producing a professionally made documentary that brings the vision to life.

Feature interviews with Filipino engineers, scientists, researchers, executives, suppliers, entrepreneurs, and technology leaders working in Silicon Valley, Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, and Singapore. Include footage of semiconductor fabrication facilities, AI research centers, advanced manufacturing plants, technology parks, and innovation campuses. Show how these ecosystems evolved over decades through sustained investments in education, research, infrastructure, entrepreneurship, and public-private collaboration.

Such a documentary would help Filipinos visualize the long-term ambition behind Pax Silica—not as a project that can be completed within a single administration, but as a national transformation that may take decades to realize. It would demonstrate that this initiative is fundamentally about preparing the Philippines for the economy of the future.

Invite Filipino professionals working abroad to share not only their technical expertise but also their personal journeys. Let them explain the knowledge they have gained, the innovations they have helped create, and the opportunities that thriving technology ecosystems have provided. Their stories can inspire young Filipinos to pursue careers in engineering, science, artificial intelligence, computer science, semiconductor technology, and advanced manufacturing.

Equally important, the documentary should explain that economic progress and environmental stewardship are not mutually exclusive. Modern semiconductor and high-technology industries operate under stringent environmental regulations, advanced waste treatment systems, water recycling technologies, emissions controls, and continuous environmental monitoring. With sound planning, effective regulation, and responsible governance, industrial development and environmental protection can progress together.

The national conversation, therefore, should not focus exclusively on environmental concerns or political debate. It should also explore how the Philippines can responsibly build an innovation-driven economy capable of competing with the world's leading industrial nations while safeguarding its natural resources.

Allow me to share a perspective shaped by my own professional experience.

I am now retired after spending much of my career working in Silicon Valley. I served as the Chief Accountant for one of the major suppliers of electronic components to the technology industry. Although my responsibilities were in finance and accounting rather than engineering, I had the opportunity to observe firsthand how an advanced technology ecosystem functions—how engineers, manufacturers, suppliers, universities, venture capital firms, financial institutions, and technology companies work together to foster innovation, create high-value employment, and sustain long-term economic growth.

That experience taught me that world-class technology ecosystems are not built overnight. They are the product of long-term vision, consistent investment, collaboration among government, industry, and academia, strong educational institutions, and a culture that encourages innovation and continuous learning.

If Pax Silica succeeds, its greatest achievement will not simply be the construction of new facilities or the attraction of foreign investment. Its true legacy will be the creation of a new generation of Filipino engineers, scientists, researchers, entrepreneurs, and globally competitive technology companies that can shape the country's economic future for decades to come. That is why this initiative deserves a national conversation that is as ambitious, informed, and forward-looking as the vision it seeks to achieve.

Honourable Minister of Commerce and Industry,
Thank you for sharing this valuable information.
Based on my understanding of the Semiconductor Manufacturing Process presented in the referenced video ( , I have explored the possibility of integrating this opportunity with Project Udyam Ganga. This concept may provide a structured framework for developing small student-led startups operating under the guidance of a leading startup or industry partner.
It is respectfully submitted that the proposed model may be integrated into Project Udyam Ganga for students of Classes IX to XII under the academic supervision of nearby colleges. Each participating school may be assigned specific stages of the manufacturing process and provided with the necessary infrastructure. Microfinancing may be facilitated through the Mini Bank proposed under Project Udyam Ganga. Where additional financial assistance is required, support may be extended through the financial mechanisms established by the competent authorities, as per applicable policies and regulations.
For implementation, one cluster may consist of four or more nearby schools supported by one nearby college. The manufacturing stages may be distributed as follows:
•	School 1: Water Manufacturing and Oxidation
•	School 2: Photolithography and Etching
•	School 3: Deposition, Ion Implantation, and Metal Wiring
•	School 4: EDS, Packaging, and Epilog
College students may be trained to mentor, supervise, and coordinate the activities undertaken by school students at each stage. The completed output from all participating schools may be consolidated and submitted to the leading startup or industry partner for quality verification, value addition, and onward supply or export, as per applicable industry standards.
The participating school students may receive stage-specific technical training, while college students may be provided with advanced training to serve as mentors, trainers, and coordinators. This framework may enable college students to lead small student startups, with overall technical guidance, quality assurance, and market linkage being provided by the leading company or startup.
Such a collaborative model may contribute to strengthening semiconductor manufacturing awareness, vocational education, entrepreneurship, industry-academia collaboration, and employment-oriented skill development at the school and college levels, if considered feasible by the competent authorities.

Looking back on this, it's astonishing how *few* of the systems in cars actually need to be computerized to work, when you start researching alternative solutions. 

Power windows and locks can be made to work with micro switches, relays, electromagnets, basic push buttons, and cheap DC motors that don't need microcontrollers. 

Anti-lock brakes originated over a century ago in purely mechanical form for aircraft landing gear. 

Traction control can be done mechanically via torque sensing differentials like those offered by Torsen, which transfer torque from wheels with lesser traction to those that have more.

Stability control could be created through reverse engineering of analog inertial navigation systems and autopilots on older aircraft, as these would correct course on their own if the craft deviated from where pilots wanted to go, all without what we'd consider a computer in the modern sense. 

O2 sensors are actually analog technology that uses voltage to communicate with the ECU, and rather than use a DAC to convert the signal to digital you can use analog circuitry to interpret and respond to it directly.

tl;dr there's other ways to build a car, but most of us don't know how to do it.

Imagine that a group of global investors approaches the Philippines and says, "We want to build here. We are prepared to invest billions of pesos over many years to help establish a world-class technology ecosystem."
That investment is not simply about constructing data centers or factories. It is about creating an ecosystem similar to Silicon Valley—an ecosystem that integrates research, education, semiconductor manufacturing, artificial intelligence, software development, advanced manufacturing, logistics, entrepreneurship, housing, transportation, finance, and thousands of supporting businesses.
For decades, millions of Filipinos have left the country in search of better opportunities abroad. Many engineers, despite their qualifications, end up accepting jobs unrelated to their profession because comparable opportunities are limited at home.

Pax Silica presents a different possibility.

Instead of Filipinos chasing opportunities overseas, the opportunities could begin coming to the Philippines. High-quality, well-paying jobs could increasingly become available here, allowing more Filipinos to build successful careers without leaving their families behind.
That is perhaps the greatest promise of this initiative—not simply economic growth, but the chance to retain Filipino talent and give young people confidence that they can build their future in their own country.
Unfortunately, much of the public discussion has focused almost exclusively on potential negative consequences. Commentators have raised concerns about environmental degradation, the exploitation of natural resources, electricity demand, water supply, food security, and other legitimate issues.
These concerns deserve careful examination and should never be ignored.
However, they should not become the only lens through which the initiative is viewed.
A balanced discussion should also ask important questions such as:
What economic opportunities could this create?
How many industries could benefit?
What educational reforms will be needed?
How can environmental risks be mitigated using proven international standards?
What lessons can be learned from countries that have successfully developed high-technology industries?
How can the Philippines maximize the benefits while minimizing the risks?
Every successful technology hub in the world—including Silicon Valley, Taiwan's semiconductor industry, South Korea, Japan, and Singapore—has faced difficult challenges involving land use, infrastructure, environmental protection, energy, and workforce development. Their success did not come from ignoring these issues, but from solving them through sound engineering, effective governance, scientific research, and long-term planning.
Pax Silica is not a project that will transform the Philippines overnight. Building a globally competitive technology ecosystem will likely take decades. That reality should encourage patience, consistent public policy, sustained investment, and broad national support rather than unrealistic expectations of immediate results.

Most importantly, we should think about the message we send to the next generation.
If young Filipinos hear only why the project might fail, they may never prepare themselves for the opportunities it could create. But if they also hear about the careers, industries, and innovations that could emerge, they may be inspired to study science, technology, engineering, and mathematics, develop globally competitive skills, and help build those industries here at home.
The choice before us is not whether to ignore the risks or to embrace blind optimism. The choice is whether we are willing to evaluate this opportunity objectively, learning from the experiences of countries that have successfully built world-class technology ecosystems.
Pax Silica should ultimately be judged not by speculation or political rhetoric, but by rigorous planning, sound environmental stewardship, transparent governance, technical expertise, and its long-term contribution to the nation's economic and technological development.
If the Philippines is serious about becoming a knowledge-based economy, this is the kind of conversation we should be having—not one driven solely by fear of what could go wrong, but one equally focused on what we must do to make it succeed for the benefit of future generations.

Rare Earth estaba vinculada con el sello de la Motown que tenía su mismo nombre. Una temprana versión de la banda, se formó en 1961, en la ciudad de Detroit, bajo el nombre de The Sunliners y durante seis años se movieron en el terreno del soul y blues. En 1967 se refundaron como Rare Earth y extendieron sus influencias al entonces naciente jazz rock (en la contraportada de su primer disco, se reivindicaban como cercanos a Blood, Sweat & Tears).[1]

La formación de Rare Earth en esta primera época, era la siguiente: Gil Bridges (vocalista, saxo, flauta y percusión), Rod Richards (guitarra y voz), John Persh (bajo y voz), Kenny James (órgano y piano) y Peter Riviera (batería y voz).

En 1970, se incorpora el percusionista Ed Guzmán (congas y pandereta) y en 1971 Ray Monette sustituye a Richards en las guitarras y Mark Olson se hace cargo del órgano tras la marcha de James.

Nuevos cambios en 1975, incorporando un segundo saxofonista y vocalista, Jerry LaCroix, que había estado en Blood, Sweat & Tears, y haciéndose cargo del bajo y batería, Reggie McBride y Barry Eugene Frost, respectivamente. Más tarde, Rivera retornaría al grupo, en su segunda etapa, sustituyendo a Frost.

Después de su disolución, dos de los miembros fundadores Gil Bridges y Peter Rivera, continuaron en el mundo de la música manteniendo una agria disputa sobre los derechos del nombre de la banda. Hoy en día Gil Bridges lidera una nueva banda con el nombre de Rare Earth, a la que durante un tiempo también estuvo ligado Ray Monette. Por su parte, Peter Rivera, en compañía de una serie de músicos provenientes de otras antiguas bandas de rock, lidera una formación denominada The Classic Rock All Stars

In the 1820s, Nicephore Niepce invented a photographic process that used Bitumen of Judea, a natural asphalt, as the first photoresist. A thin coating of the bitumen on a sheet of metal, glass or stone became less soluble where it was exposed to light; the unexposed parts could then be rinsed away with a suitable solvent, baring the material beneath, which was then chemically etched in an acid bath to produce a printing plate. The light-sensitivity of bitumen was very poor and very long exposures were required, but despite the later introduction of more sensitive alternatives, its low cost and superb resistance to strong acids prolonged its commercial life into the early 20th century.

In 1940, Oskar Süß created a positive photoresist by using diazonaphthoquinone, which worked in the opposite manner: the coating was initially insoluble and was rendered soluble where it was exposed to light.[4] In 1954, Louis Plambeck Jr. developed the Dycryl polymeric letterpress plate, which made the platemaking process faster.[5] Development of photoresists used to be carried out in batches of wafers (batch processing) dipped into a bath of developer, but modern process offerings do development one wafer at a time (single wafer processing) to improve process control.[6]

This is what I cannot accept about the Philippines.
We have economists and highly educated technocrats. We have world-class architects and urban planners like Palafox. We have IRRI in Los Baños, one of the world's leading rice research institutions. We certainly do not lack intelligent Filipinos or technical knowledge.
Yet somehow, we still cannot consistently produce enough of some of our most basic food requirements without relying heavily on imports. Rice, onions, sugar, and pork repeatedly become national supply and price problems. Metro Manila still struggles with something as basic as garbage management.
And now, every rainy season, we seem prepared to accept that huge portions of Bulacan and Pampanga will simply go underwater.
I refuse to accept that as normal.
A typhoon is a natural event. Heavy rain is a natural event. But when the same communities flood repeatedly because rivers are silted, waterways are obstructed, drainage is inadequate, pumps are insufficient, floodgates are poorly maintained, and garbage blocks waterways, that is no longer purely a natural disaster.
That is also a failure of planning, execution, maintenance, and governance.
The frustrating thing is that the Philippines does not lack expertise. What we lack is the institutional ability to take good ideas, execute them properly, maintain them for decades, and hold people accountable when they fail.
That is the real tragedy.
We know how to grow food. We know how to design cities. We know how to build drainage systems, pumping stations, dams, floodways, and proper waste-management systems. Other countries use the same technologies.
Yet year after year, we act surprised when the same places flood again.
Bulacan and Pampanga are too economically important, too populated, and too close to Metro Manila for chronic flooding to be treated as an unavoidable part of the rainy season. At some point, accepting the problem becomes more expensive than fixing it.
This is no longer just an inconvenience. It damages businesses, destroys crops and property, disrupts workers and transportation, raises food prices, discourages investment, and ultimately reduces the country's productivity and standard of living.
The Philippines does not have an intelligence problem. It has an execution and accountability problem.

Nickel ore processing facilities (both pyrometallurgical- and hydrometallurgical-based techniques) would not be compatible with the declared vision of a "green" industrial-residential hub of the New Clark City. These typical hydro- and pyro-metallurgical processing such as high pressure acid leaching, or HPAL, for producing intermediate nickel compounds for EV batteries, and the high temp rotary-kiln electric furnace, or RKEF,  for producing ferronickels (used in stainless steel production) of lateritic/saprolitic nickel ores generate significant negative environmental effects, that it makes more sense to build these facilities adjacent to the actual mining sites (Caraga region of Mindanao, Palawan, and Zambales) where they can be best managed. In fact, the only two currently active nickel ore processing HPAL plants in the Phils (both associated with the Japanese company, Sumitomo Mining) are located at the mining sites in Rio Tuba, Palawan and in Taganito, Surigao del Norte. The Phil government needs to be clear about what metal ore processing industries and exactly where they would host these industries that are being planned as components of the Pax Silica project. Moreover, since the current electronics/semiconductor industry demands are less than 1% of the global nickel production (with stainless steel at 65%, EV batteries at 12%-20%, and specialty alloys/aerospace at about 12% of global demands), the Phil government should strategically prioritize which metals processing facilities it will admit within the Pax Silica framework that serves the greatest good for the Filipino people. There is still a whole host of processing industries downstream from the hydro- and pyro-metallurgical processing of nickel ores to turn them into the correct types of nickel compounds, pure metal, and nickel alloys that are then used for semiconductor manufacturing. The government needs to carefully evaluate and vet which mineral processing industries it should engage with within the Pax Silica initiative to protect the interests of the Filipinos.

Companies invest to build businesses, and they should hire people based on the skills and qualifications required for the job. Some companies will naturally provide training, apprenticeships and opportunities for employees to develop their skills over time, especially when retaining experienced workers benefits the company. That's how advanced economies work. They don't demand that every foreign company hire local workers regardless of whether they have the necessary qualifications. If a country lacks enough semiconductor engineers, AI specialists, technicians or other highly specialized professionals, foreign experts may initially fill those positions while the domestic education and training system catches up. Over time, more locals can qualify, gain experience and move into those positions.
And we shouldn't expect foreigners to be replaced simply because a foreign investor establishes an AI or semiconductor business here. If a Filipino applicant is qualified, they should compete for the position and have the opportunity to advance. If they aren't qualified yet, the answer is to improve our education and training - not to demand that companies lower their standards. That's meritocracy. The goal should be to make Filipinos qualified enough to compete for these jobs, not to guarantee jobs regardless of competence.
